source: A word concerning an incident in the last chapter.

According to the invariable usage of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship, with the headsman or whale-killer as temporary steersman, and the harpooneer or whale-fastener pulling the foremost oar, the one known as the harpooneer-oar. Now it needs a strong, nervous arm to strike the first iron into the fish; for often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy implement has to be flung to the distance of twenty or thirty feet. But however prolonged and exhausting the chase, the harpooneer is expected to pull his oar meanwhile to the uttermost; indeed, he is expected to set an example of superhuman activity to the rest, not only by incredible rowing, but by repeated loud and intrepid exclamations; and what it is to keep shouting at the top of one’s compass, while all the other muscles are strained and half started—what that is none know but those who have tried it. For one, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time. In this straining, bawling state, then, with his back to the fish, all at once the exhausted harpooneer hears the exciting cry—“Stand up, and give it to him!” He now has to drop and secure his oar, turn round on his centre half way, seize his harpoon from the crotch, and with what little strength may remain, he essays to pitch it somehow into the whale. No wonder, taking the whole fleet of whalemen in a body, that out of fifty fair chances for a dart, not five are successful; no wonder that so many hapless harpooneers are madly cursed and disrated; no wonder that some of them actually burst their blood-vessels in the boat; no wonder that some sperm whalemen are absent four years with four barrels; no wonder that to many ship owners, whaling is but a losing concern; for it is the harpooneer that makes the voyage, and if you take the breath out of his body how can you expect to find it there when most wanted!

Again, if the dart be successful, then at the second critical instant, that is, when the whale starts to run, the boatheader and harpooneer likewise start to running fore and aft, to the imminent jeopardy of themselves and every one else. It is then they change places; and the headsman, the chief officer of the little craft, takes his proper station in the bows of the boat.

Now, I care not who maintains the contrary, but all this is both foolish and unnecessary. The headsman should stay in the bows from first to last; he should both dart the harpoon and the lance, and no rowing whatever should be expected of him, except under circumstances obvious to any fisherman. I know that this would sometimes involve a slight loss of speed in the chase; but long experience in various whalemen of more than one nation has convinced me that in the vast majority of failures in the fishery, it has not by any means been so much the speed of the whale as the before described exhaustion of the harpooneer that has caused them.
To insure the greatest efficiency in the dart, the harpooneers of this world must start to their feet from out of idleness, and not from out of toil.

modern_en.title: Chapter 62 — The Dart
paragraphs: A word concerning an incident in the last chapter.

According to the invariable custom of the fishery, the whale-boat pushes off from the ship with the headsman, or whale-killer, as temporary steersman, and the harpooner, or whale-fastener, pulling the foremost oar, the one known as the harpooner-oar. Now it takes a strong, nervy arm to strike the first iron into the fish; for often, in what is called a long dart, the heavy implement has to be flung a distance of twenty or thirty feet. But however long and exhausting the chase, the harpooner is expected to pull his oar to the utmost all the while; indeed, he is expected to set the rest an example of superhuman activity, not only by incredible rowing, but by repeated loud and fearless shouts; and what it is to keep shouting at the top of your voice while every other muscle is strained and half wrenched out of place — that no one knows but those who have tried it. For my part, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time. In this straining, bawling state, then, with his back to the fish, the exhausted harpooner all at once hears the exciting cry — "Stand up, and give it to him!" He now has to drop and secure his oar, turn halfway round on his center, seize his harpoon from the crotch, and with what little strength may remain, try to pitch it somehow into the whale. No wonder, taking the whole fleet of whalemen together, that out of fifty fair chances for a dart, not five are successful; no wonder that so many luckless harpooners are madly cursed and demoted; no wonder that some of them actually burst their blood-vessels in the boat; no wonder that some sperm whalemen are gone four years with four barrels; no wonder that to many shipowners whaling is nothing but a losing business; for it is the harpooner who makes the voyage, and if you take the breath out of his body, how can you expect to find it there when it is most wanted!

Then again, if the dart hits home, at the second critical moment — when the whale starts to run — the boatheader and harpooner likewise start running fore and aft, putting themselves and everyone else in imminent danger. That is when they swap places, and the headsman, the chief officer of the little craft, takes his proper post in the bow.

Now, I don't care who says otherwise: all this is both foolish and unnecessary. The headsman should stay in the bow from start to finish. He should throw both the harpoon and the lance, and no rowing at all should be expected of him, except in circumstances any fisherman would recognize. I know this would sometimes cost a little speed in the chase; but the long experience of many whalemen of more than one nation has convinced me that in the great majority of failures in the fishery, the cause has by no means been so much the whale's speed as the harpooner's exhaustion that I described earlier.
To make the dart as effective as possible, the harpooners of this world must spring to their feet from rest, not from hard labor.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 62 — Kastet
paragraphs: Et ord om en hændelse i det sidste kapitel.

Efter fangstens uforanderlige sædvane lægger hvalbåden fra skibet med bådføreren, eller hvaldræberen, som midlertidig rorgænger, og harpunéren, eller hvalfæsteren, ved den forreste åre, den, der kaldes harpunéråren. Nu kræver det en stærk, senet arm at slå det første jern ind i fisken; for ofte, i det, der kaldes et langt kast, må det tunge redskab slynges en afstand på tyve eller tredive fod. Men hvor lang og udmattende jagten end er, forventes det, at harpunéren hele tiden ror af alle kræfter; ja, han forventes at give de andre et eksempel på overmenneskelig virksomhed, ikke blot ved utrolig roning, men ved gentagne, høje og uforfærdede råb; og hvad det vil sige at blive ved med at råbe af sine lungers fulde kraft, mens alle andre muskler er spændt til det yderste og halvt vredet ud af led — det ved ingen undtagen dem, der har prøvet det. Jeg for min part kan ikke brøle særlig hjerteligt og arbejde særlig hensynsløst på én gang. I denne anstrengte, brølende tilstand hører den udmattede harpunér så med ryggen til fisken pludselig det opildnende råb — »Op med dig, og giv ham den!« Nu må han give slip på og fastgøre sin åre, dreje sig halvt rundt på sin midte, gribe sin harpun fra gaflen og med den ringe styrke, der måtte være tilbage, på en eller anden måde prøve at kaste den ind i hvalen. Det er intet under, når man tager hele flåden af hvalfangere under ét, at ud af halvtreds gode chancer for et kast lykkes der ikke fem; intet under, at så mange uheldige harpunérer bliver vanvittigt udskældt og degraderet; intet under, at nogle af dem faktisk sprænger blodkar i båden; intet under, at nogle kaskelotfangere er væk i fire år og kommer hjem med fire tønder; intet under, at hvalfangst for mange skibsredere ikke er andet end en tabsgivende forretning; for det er harpunéren, der gør rejsen, og hvis man tager pusten fra hans krop, hvordan kan man så forvente at finde den der, når den trænges allermest!

Dernæst, hvis kastet rammer, begynder bådføreren og harpunéren ved det andet kritiske øjeblik — når hvalen sætter i løb — ligeledes at løbe forude og agterud, så de bringer sig selv og alle andre i overhængende fare. Det er da, de bytter plads, og bådføreren, den lille båds øverste officer, indtager sin rette post i stævnen.

Nu er jeg ligeglad med, hvem der siger noget andet: Alt dette er både tåbeligt og unødvendigt. Bådføreren bør blive i stævnen fra først til sidst. Han bør kaste både harpunen og lansen, og der bør slet ikke forventes roning af ham, undtagen under omstændigheder, enhver fisker ville kende. Jeg ved, at det nogle gange ville koste lidt fart i jagten; men mange hvalfangeres lange erfaring, fra mere end én nation, har overbevist mig om, at årsagen til langt de fleste fejlslagne forsøg i fangsten på ingen måde har været så meget hvalens fart som harpunérens udmattelse, som jeg har beskrevet før.
For at gøre kastet så virkningsfuldt som muligt må verdens harpunérer springe op fra hvile, ikke fra hårdt arbejde.
